# The Keeper of Harrow Point

The bottle came in on a Tuesday, which was the kind of day the sea reserved for small miracles.

Elias Vane had kept the Harrow Point light for eleven years. Eleven years of climbing the one hundred and twelve iron steps each evening, eleven years of trimming the wick, eleven years of watching the fog roll in from the north like a slow grey animal. He had stopped counting the days the same way he had stopped counting the ships. They all looked the same in the dark. They all needed the same thing: a steady, honest flame.

So when the tide dragged a green glass bottle up against the rocks below the gallery, he almost missed it. Almost. But Elias had eleven years of looking for things that didn't belong, and the bottle caught the last of the afternoon sun like a small trapped star.

He hauled it up the steps with his oil-stained hands. The sand inside was coarse and pale, not the dark volcanic grit of Harrow Point. He shook it. Something solid clinked against the glass.

It took him three days to open it. Not because the cork was stuck—though it was, swollen with salt and years—but because he couldn't bring himself to. The bottle sat on his workbench between the logbook and the tin of tinned peaches, and every time he passed it, he felt the particular guilt of a man who has been given a secret and is choosing to keep it.
